prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

For instance, one participant expressed their priorities clearly: “I just want safe and protected bike lanes, safe pedestrian crossings, wider and shaded footpaths, and raised crossings at intersections, so cars have to go over the raised area instead of pedestrians having to go down onto the road” (M, 36). The need for broader changes to address these issues was repeatedly highlighted, as another participant noted: “Footpaths are too narrow and poorly maintained, there are not enough safe crossings with islands, cyclists should always have permanent, dedicated lanes wherever there is a road, and they should really fix the train bridges so there are no at-road level crossings. More pedestrian refuge islands is also a brilliant opportunity to plant more trees” (F, 31). These suggestions underline the interconnected benefits of safety improvements and environmental enhancements. Participants consistently linked infrastructure upgrades to safety and justice, reflecting a belief that physical changes to the transport system are foundational for achieving equity. One participant succinctly summarised this perspective: “The government desperately needs to improve the pedestrian and cyclist safety situations. Footpaths are too narrow and poorly maintained, and there are not enough safe crossings with islands” (F, 33). Another added, “Prioritise infrastructure for vulnerable road users so we don’t have to share with any motor vehicles” (M, 52). Collectively, these responses reflect a strong consensus that redesigning infrastructure is essential for creating a safer and fairer transport system that can effectively integrate CAVs. 3.5.3. Inclusivity and accessibility Codes such as “inclusive design,” “accessible vehicles,” and “no burden on VRUs” reflected participants’ concerns about marginalised groups, particularly people with disabilities, the elderly, and those without access to wearable technology. Concerns around inclusivity and accessibility were prominent, with participants firmly rejecting policies that placed the burden of adaptation on VRUs. Many criticised proposals requiring VRUs to use reflective clothing, specific apps, or wearable devices to ensure their visibility to CAVs. One participant voiced their frustration: “Pedestrians should NOT have to wear something so that these cars can see them… If the robot can’t see pedestrians, then it should not be allowed on the road” (NB, 18). Sidewalk paving: It shall meet the requirements of stability, anti-slip performance, flatness, ecological environmental protection, and urban landscape. Its design shall be practical, economical, aesthetically pleasing, and durable, and shall be designed for permeability in accordance with sponge city requirements. Guidance and directional signs may be added to the paving; signs shall be appropriately scaled and clearly informative. 2. Tactile paving: The color of tactile paving should contrast with the color of adjacent sidewalk paving and be coordinated with the surrounding landscape. The surface of tactile paving profiles shall have anti-slip functionality. The width should be 0.3 m–0.6 m, and the tactile pattern shall protrude 4 mm above the road surface. Tactile paving shall be laid continuously and shall avoid obstacles such as trees (tree pits), utility poles, and guy wires. Figure 4.3-5 Example of tactile paving 3. Curb stones: These shall be designed in accordance with road class, construction scale, landscape environment, and usage requirements. Sidewalks must be provided with curb ramps at all intersections and at the entrances/exits of residential communities and institutions fronting the street. The height difference between the curb stone and the road surface shall not exceed 1 cm. At pedestrian crossings, the centerline of the curb-ramp opening should align with the centerline of the crosswalk. At road intersections, curb ramps are recommended to adopt a full-width, single-sided ramp descending to the bottom. 4. Tree pits / tree grates: Their dimensions shall be designed in coordination with the sidewalk paving, forming a certain proportional modular relationship. The paved surface of the tree pit / tree grate should be flush with the sidewalk paving. Tree grates should preferably use fiberglass grating, eco-friendly rubber, stone paving, and similar materials. In parks, squares, commercial pedestrian streets, and other leisure activity areas, tree pits should be designed in combination with seating, or as compact / multifunctional designs that provide seating functions. The paved surface of the manhole cover shall be flush with the sidewalk paving surface, and the height difference shall not exceed 1 cm. As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups

Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability

Comfort

- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability

Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):

For instance, one participant expressed their priorities clearly: “I just want safe and protected bike lanes, safe pedestrian crossings, wider and shaded footpaths, and raised crossings at intersections, so cars have to go over the raised area instead of pedestrians having to go down onto the road” (M, 36). The need for broader changes to address these issues was repeatedly highlighted, as another participant noted: “Footpaths are too narrow and poorly maintained, there are not enough safe crossings with islands, cyclists should always have permanent, dedicated lanes wherever there is a road, and they should really fix the train bridges so there are no at-road level crossings. More pedestrian refuge islands is also a brilliant opportunity to plant more trees” (F, 31). These suggestions underline the interconnected benefits of safety improvements and environmental enhancements. Participants consistently linked infrastructure upgrades to safety and justice, reflecting a belief that physical changes to the transport system are foundational for achieving equity. One participant succinctly summarised this perspective: “The government desperately needs to improve the pedestrian and cyclist safety situations. Footpaths are too narrow and poorly maintained, and there are not enough safe crossings with islands” (F, 33). Another added, “Prioritise infrastructure for vulnerable road users so we don’t have to share with any motor vehicles” (M, 52). Collectively, these responses reflect a strong consensus that redesigning infrastructure is essential for creating a safer and fairer transport system that can effectively integrate CAVs. 3.5.3. Inclusivity and accessibility Codes such as “inclusive design,” “accessible vehicles,” and “no burden on VRUs” reflected participants’ concerns about marginalised groups, particularly people with disabilities, the elderly, and those without access to wearable technology. Concerns around inclusivity and accessibility were prominent, with participants firmly rejecting policies that placed the burden of adaptation on VRUs. Many criticised proposals requiring VRUs to use reflective clothing, specific apps, or wearable devices to ensure their visibility to CAVs. One participant voiced their frustration: “Pedestrians should NOT have to wear something so that these cars can see them… If the robot can’t see pedestrians, then it should not be allowed on the road” (NB, 18). Figure 4.3-4 Example of Walkway Lights 4.3.3 Pavement Surfacing 1. Sidewalk paving: It shall meet the requirements of stability, anti-slip performance, flatness, ecological environmental protection, and urban landscape. Its design shall be practical, economical, aesthetically pleasing, and durable, and shall be designed for permeability in accordance with sponge city requirements. Guidance and directional signs may be added to the paving; signs shall be appropriately scaled and clearly informative. 2. Tactile paving: The color of tactile paving should contrast with the color of adjacent sidewalk paving and be coordinated with the surrounding landscape. The surface of tactile paving profiles shall have anti-slip functionality. The width should be 0.3 m–0.6 m, and the tactile pattern shall protrude 4 mm above the road surface. Tactile paving shall be laid continuously and shall avoid obstacles such as trees (tree pits), utility poles, and guy wires. Figure 4.3-5 Example of tactile paving 3. Curb stones: These shall be designed in accordance with road class, construction scale, landscape environment, and usage requirements. Sidewalks must be provided with curb ramps at all intersections and at the entrances/exits of residential communities and institutions fronting the street. The height difference between the curb stone and the road surface shall not exceed 1 cm. At pedestrian crossings, the centerline of the curb-ramp opening should align with the centerline of the crosswalk. At road intersections, curb ramps are recommended to adopt a full-width, single-sided ramp descending to the bottom. 4. Tree pits / tree grates: Their dimensions shall be designed in coordination with the sidewalk paving, forming a certain proportional modular relationship. The paved surface of the tree pit / tree grate should be flush with the sidewalk paving. Tree grates should preferably use fiberglass grating, eco-friendly rubber, stone paving, and similar materials. In parks, squares, commercial pedestrian streets, and other leisure activity areas, tree pits should be designed in combination with seating, or as compact / multifunctional designs that provide seating functions. Figure 4.3-6 Example of tree pits / tree grates 5. Manhole covers: All types of manhole covers shall comply with the relevant standards in Manhole Covers (GB/T 23858-2009). The paved surface of the manhole cover shall be flush with the sidewalk paving surface, and the height difference shall not exceed 1 cm. Concealed manhole covers may be used; the decorative surface layer shall be unified with the road paving. Manhole covers with distinctive patterns may also be used. They are usually installed along sidewalks, as well as in parks, squares, tourist attractions, and similar areas.
